name: Territorial churches formed
description: Lutheran territorial churches developed in German lands following the Reformation.
narrative: Lutheran territorial churches developed in German lands following the Reformation. Princes and civic governments helped organize Lutheran worship, schools, and ministry in different German lands. Political settlements such as the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 shaped the setting in which territorial churches developed. This node groups multiple churches rather than naming one denomination founded that year. Emigration later carried several of these traditions to North America, where churches adopted new organizational forms.

key_figures.name: Martin Luther
key_figures.summary: A German reformer whose teaching on justification, catechesis, and sacramental life shaped the Lutheran confessional tradition.

key_figures.name: Philipp Melanchthon
key_figures.role: confessional author; not sole organizer of every territorial church
key_figures.summary: A scholar and colleague of Luther who was the principal author of the Augsburg Confession, helping explain Lutheran teaching in a public confessional form.

name: State churches established
description: Scandinavian state churches adopted Lutheranism in the Reformation era.
narrative: Scandinavian state churches adopted Lutheranism in the Reformation era. Lutheran reform entered Scandinavian kingdoms through preaching, teaching, and royal action. The resulting churches retained different national histories and forms of oversight. The dataset’s 1536 marker should not imply that all Scandinavian churches were founded or reformed simultaneously. Migration connected these national traditions to American Lutheran communities, especially through bodies that later entered the ELCA.

key_figures.name: Hans Tausen
key_figures.summary: A Danish preacher influenced by study with Luther who helped introduce Lutheran reform in Denmark.

key_figures.name: Mikael Agricola
key_figures.summary: A Finnish reformer and translator whose work helped make biblical and religious texts accessible in Finnish.

name: German immigrant roots
description: LCMS was founded by German immigrants from territorial churches in Germany.
narrative: LCMS was founded by German immigrants from territorial churches in Germany. German immigrant and mission communities formed a synod to preserve Lutheran teaching and coordinate ministry in the United States. C. F. W. Walther became its first president. The church developed educational and mission institutions while insisting on doctrinal agreement. Disputes in the 1970s led some congregations into the AELC, later an ELCA predecessor; this was a division within American Lutheran history, not the origin of Lutheranism itself.

description: Scandinavian immigrant traditions helped shape ELCA predecessor churches over generations. This is inherited influence through intervening American bodies, not direct institutional formation in 1987.
narrative: Scandinavian immigrant traditions helped shape ELCA predecessor churches over generations. This is inherited influence through intervening American bodies, not direct institutional formation in 1987. The constituting convention met in 1987, and the ELCA began operations in 1988.
